The research default is `gpt-5.6-luna`, selected in `AI_MODELS` in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`. Model names are not read from environment variables. Research runs in two stages. Discovery finds up to six competitors from the startup's product and target customer rather than its industry label: the model first writes short shopper phrases for the product and customer, then searches at least four times, recent campaign news first, for companies that have run New York subway, billboard, bus shelter, LinkNYC or wild-posting campaigns and that sell a substitute or target the same customer. Government campaigns, non-profits and media owners are excluded. Discovery also records every campaign its searches turn up, including ones that name no place, using recent campaigns and the current year in its searches. It cannot finish with fewer than three competitors until it has made five searches. Discovery has twelve model steps and a 60-second deadline. Each competitor then gets its own placement search for stations, street addresses, neighbourhoods and dates, told which campaigns are already recorded, with eight model steps and 65 seconds, all running concurrently within a 165-second total deadline; the Route Handler has a 170-second deadline. One finding can name up to six places, and each place becomes its own row. Each competitor can contribute up to six rows with a map location and three without, counted separately so that findings without a place cannot crowd out located ones. A run reports at most 54 rows. The first model step of each stage requires hosted search, and each response allows up to eight hosted tool calls, in parallel. Typed tools reject URLs absent from the run's research sources. Hosted-search-only responses continue into reporting within the same step budget. The model extracts the evidence; source membership does not independently fact-check its summary. Dates are classified as current, historical or unknown. Only matched subway stations or street addresses with a confirmed date range covering today affect competition. Geocoded areas and unknown or historical dates remain visible as markers without lowering gap scores. Other findings stay visible with source links, evidence and locations. A search returning no campaigns does not establish that competitors are absent. The sample recording contains five competitors and twenty campaign findings, nine of them with map locations. Re-capture it from `tools/` with `uv run python -c 'from tools.sources.competitor_run import load; load(refresh=True)'` while the web app runs. The budgeting app found Openigloo, StreetEasy and RentHop, and its Openigloo marathon campaign produced approximate markers at Fort Greene, Williamsburg, Greenpoint, Park Slope and the Upper East Side. The dating app found Hinge, The League, Tinder, Plenty of Fish and HUD, with 18 campaign findings, 10 of them on the map. None of the findings had confirmed current dates, so none lowered gap scores. In the browser, the sample brief showed the rows and the map note with no console errors. All 49 tests, web lint, typecheck and build passed. Verified earlier, on 8 November 2026 in commit `Find competitors from the product and customer, then search each for placements`: live runs of four briefs each completed in 27 to 43 seconds. The dating app found Plenty of Fish, Hinge, The League, Bumble, Cerca and HUD, with 12 campaign findings, four of them at matched subway stations. The budgeting app found Openigloo, StreetEasy and Job Today; the pizza delivery service found Slice, Seamless and WoodSpoon; the telehealth service found Roman. None of the findings had confirmed current dates, so none lowered gap scores. In the browser, the sample brief listed Openigloo, StreetEasy and RentHop with seven campaign findings and no console errors. All 32 tests, web lint, typecheck and build passed. In a scratch comparison over 12 test briefs, searching named direct competitors found no campaigns at a named station or street address for any brief, and this two-stage search found them for 10 of 12. Verified earlier, on 7 November 2026 in `2a85115`: live research and production fallback flows above; eight focused tests for CSV parsing, source checks, station matching, dates, gap effects, split SDK stream chunks, interruption and cancellation; HTTP 400 for invalid briefs and 413 for oversized briefs; web lint, typecheck and build; Python Ruff checks; station data and recording present in the production deployment trace. Serves G-Research. Search and page reading alone do not establish the browser-control workflow for Wordsmith.
 - Planned: verified placement prices and minimum spends, and competitors' stores and offices as separate presence evidence. Serves G-Research and HRT. Browser control remains unbuilt for Wordsmith.
 - Built: shared model and provider setup in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`, using the installed SDK provider registry. Code defaults select OpenAI `gpt-5.6-luna` for research and Gateway Jev for audience decisions. The research adapter bundles the model, search tool, options, credential checks, source decoding and provider errors. Unsupported research providers are rejected until a compatible search adapter is added. Model environment variables have no effect; `.env.example` lists credentials only. GPT-5.6 Luna selection was verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Use GPT-5.6 Luna for competitor research`: all 13 tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. A live smoke test returned competitor findings and streamed search progress. Verified on 7 November 2026 in `f0e401d`: all 13 focused tests passed, including registry resolution, model-environment independence, credential separation, source decoding and unsupported research-provider rejection. Web lint, typecheck and build passed. In the browser, the sample showed "weighted by Jev" and completed research with no verified competitors and no console errors while the old model variable was set to an invalid value. Serves G-Research and HRT.

===================================================================

@@ -7,9 +7,9 @@

Cut on 7 November 2026 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports.
 - Cut: airport placement ranking per startup. Ranks UK and EU airport placements by how well each airport's route and airline mix matches the startup's target customer, with published or estimated prices and a sent enquiry; two startups are compared side by side in the demo. Serves G-Research and Wordsmith. Cut on 7 November 2026 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports.
-- Built: onboarding form and results page, in `web/`, with live audience scoring and competitor research. Placement pricing remains mocked. The form is a fill-in-the-blank passage, "Our company is … in …. We want to reach … who would pay $… per …, and we can spend $… a month on ads in …", ending in a city menu whose only city is New York; all five boroughs are mapped without being listed. The results are a map of New York's census tracts with Customers and Competitors tabs, a Gap tab once qualifying campaigns are found, a legend and clickable campaign markers at matched stations, addresses and approximate areas. Each marker shows its competitor's logo, loaded from the competitor's own website, and falls back to initials when the site's icon cannot be fetched; each campaign row in the Competitors tab shows the same logo. Solid markers identify current or recent campaigns with a station or address match; dashed markers identify approximate, historical or undated campaigns. Markers open no popups: hovering a campaign marker highlights its row in the Competitors tab, clicking it switches to that tab and scrolls to the row, and clicking a row's location moves the map to the marker. Each mapped row shows the data-source attribution. The placements to buy are numbered markers that match their numbers in the list, shown on the Gap and Competitors layers. Without a Gap tab they also show on the Customers layer, where they are listed; with one, the Customers layer omits them. They are chosen from observed gaps when locations of campaigns from the past 12 months are available, or from audience fit otherwise. Hovering a placement on the map or in the list highlights it in both, clicking a row moves the map to it and, on phones where the map sits above the column, scrolls back up to the map, and clicking a marker scrolls the list to its row. Tabs above the results column pick the layer for both the map and the column, in the order Customers, Competitors, Gap. Gap appears only once a campaign from the past 12 months has a station or address match. Customers opens at the start; when Gap appears it opens by itself unless another tab was clicked. Switching tabs slides the highlighted tab across, and the map's colours change at once. The column shows only that layer's sections: Gap has the 5 biggest observed gaps and up to 12 placements to buy, Customers has the 5 tracts with the most target customers, the up to 12 placements when there is no Gap tab, and the weighted tract columns, strongest first, with those that count against the customer marked "less likely", and Competitors has the competitors, each with its logo on the right of the row, and their ads, with the agent's latest step while it searches a note counting ads without a reliable location match and so absent from the map, and a separate note counting ads that run across the city or a borough. Ads with no fixed location are labelled citywide or borough-wide on their row, and the map's legend counts citywide campaigns as not pinned. Hovering a tract on the map names it and shows the current layer's value for it, and hovering a trait under Customers shows its exact weight in place of its measure. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Add hover values to tract boxes and trait bars`: web lint, typecheck and build passed; the hover tooltips were not checked in a browser. On the form, the whole background spins once every 30 seconds, sweeping colour through the edges the form card leaves visible, and its four coloured blobs each drift on their own loop of 7 to 10 seconds, moving up to 50% of the screen's larger side and growing by up to 40%. Submitting the form moves the whole results view upward from below the screen over 1.2 seconds while the same spin and drift play 12 times faster, so the background turns at 144 degrees per second, with the form visible behind it until the movement finishes. The speed-up continues from the background's current position rather than restarting, and Edit returns it to normal speed. Reduced-motion preferences stop the spin and drift and skip the visible movement. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Speed up the form background during the results transition`: the spin went from 25 degrees to 29 at the click with no jump, then turned about 65 degrees in the next 400 milliseconds; all five animations ran 12 times faster during the slide and returned to normal after Edit; screenshots 10 seconds apart on the form showed the red and yellow moving from the bottom-left corner to the bottom centre; the browser had no console errors, and web lint, typecheck and build passed. Earlier, on 8 November 2026 in commit `Speed up gradient rotation during results transition`, desktop and 390-by-844 mobile checks showed a 1.2-second slide with no horizontal overflow. The results fill the window: the map fills the left two thirds and stays in view while the column scrolls in the right third, and on phones the map sits on top at 55% of the screen height. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Animate results upward after form submission`: desktop and 390-by-844 mobile browser checks confirmed that the results and their content move together, settle at the top without horizontal overflow, and preserve the form answers on Edit. Reduced motion completed immediately, invalid amounts blocked submission, and the browser had no console errors. Web lint, typecheck and build passed. The column opens with a one-line summary of the brief and an Edit button that brings the form back with its answers kept. Submitting a completely empty form runs the sample dating-app brief with an $8,000 monthly budget in New York. Entering any field or changing a dropdown keeps full required-field and numeric-pattern validation. There is no separate `/map` route. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Use sample defaults for empty form submissions`: a blank submission showed the sample map and 12 placements; each individually filled field and a changed payment dropdown blocked incomplete submission; numeric patterns still blocked invalid amounts; a complete custom brief submitted its own values and Edit kept them; `/map` returned 404. The browser had no console errors, and all 26 tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. The sample brief changed to the dating app on 8 November 2026; its recorded run holds five competitors and twenty ads, nine with map locations, and the blank-form flow was not re-checked in a browser after the change. Faked: placement costs, minimum spends are invented. Real: the audience fit scores are weighted sums of the real scaled tract columns, and the placements are real kiosks and shelters selected across eligible tracts in descending observed gap-score order when campaigns from the past 12 months have precise locations, or descending audience fit otherwise, with one per tract and at least 500 metres between them. The column weights come from Jev through AI Gateway when `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` is set in `web/.env.local`, or on a Vercel deployment through its OIDC token: one request asks a five-level score question per column, from strongly against to strongly for, and each weight runs from -1 to 1, the probability-weighted level. Without either, or when Jev fails or takes over 20 seconds, the weights come from keyword matching on the target customer, and the Customers tab says so. Verified on 8 November 2026 with the sample brief: the Customers tab said "weighted by Jev", and the scoring request, Jev plus the tract arithmetic, took 892 ms. For "young professionals in tech who rent with roommates", the strongest weights were jobs in information (+0.94), residents aged 20 to 34 (+0.89) and median age (-0.83). Jev isn't on AI Gateway's free tier, so the key's Vercel team needs purchased AI Gateway Credits, and a card Vercel can verify. The browser computes competition per tract from its distance to each current or recent campaign's matched station or street address, falling to about a third at 1 km, and the gap as audience fit times one minus competition; that formula is a first version, not a decision. The UI imports audience scoring, streamed competitor research and placement lookup through `web/src/lib/api.ts`, with types in `web/src/lib/contract.ts`. Placements appear after audience scoring and are re-ranked when research finishes. On 7 November 2026, the live energy-drink flow returned three competitors and three source-linked campaign findings. Their dates or station locations were unknown, so none lowered the gap scores. The production sample fallback showed three recorded competitors and its capture-date label; a different brief received no recorded findings. Both browser flows had no console errors. Verified in `2a85115`. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Show competitor logos in the list and on campaign markers`: web lint, typecheck, build and all 32 tests passed, and the logo endpoint returned a PNG for each of the sample run's three competitors. The logos were not checked in a browser. Serves G-Research and HRT.

 - Built: a settings menu (gear button, bottom right) with experimental interface options saved in the browser: sharp corners (every border radius 1px), percentile classes on or off (on paints four classes above the 50th percentile and leaves the bottom half clear; off is the earlier smooth ramp), a cost-estimate switch (on by default; shows the invented price per customer, sorts placements by it and tags the lowest; off shows no prices and lists by area), and a colour palette. Classic is selected by default and listed first. The teal and coral palette is ink text (#12211F, #5B6B69, #8A9694) on #FAFAF8 with #E3E8E7 dividers, a teal ramp (#BFE0DC #7FC2BA #2F8F86 #0B5450) and a coral accent (#F2603D, darker #C9431F); teal appears only in the map fill, the active layer tab and the legend bar. Teal and coral, blue and lime, purple and amber, and a colour-blind navy palette are the alternatives. Placement markers are 24px accent circles with a white ring, 30px and darker when selected, and merge into numbered groups when they overlap at the current zoom; the map frames the placements when they first arrive. Most customers lists the five neighbourhoods with the most tracts in the top 3%, with tract counts. Verified on 8 November 2026 in headless Chrome. Not an agreed product decision, only options to compare.
 - Built: competitor research with the Vercel AI SDK's `ToolLoopAgent`, OpenAI directly through `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and hosted web search and page reading. The research default is `gpt-5.6-luna`, selected in `AI_MODELS` in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`. Model names are not read from environment variables. Research runs in two stages. Discovery finds up to six competitors from the startup's product and target customer rather than its industry label: the model first writes short shopper phrases for the product and customer, then searches at least four times, recent campaign news first, for companies that have run New York subway, billboard, bus shelter, LinkNYC or wild-posting campaigns and that sell a substitute or target the same customer. Government campaigns, non-profits and media owners are excluded. Discovery also records every campaign its searches turn up, including ones that name no place, using recent campaigns and the current year in its searches. It cannot finish with fewer than three competitors until it has made five searches. Discovery has twelve model steps and a 60-second deadline. Each competitor then gets its own placement search for stations, street addresses, neighbourhoods and dates, told which campaigns are already recorded, with eight model steps and 65 seconds, all running concurrently within a 165-second total deadline; the Route Handler has a 170-second deadline. One finding can name up to six places, and each place becomes its own row. Each competitor can contribute up to six rows with a map location and three without, counted separately so that findings without a place cannot crowd out located ones. A run reports at most 54 rows. The first model step of each stage requires hosted search, and each response allows up to eight hosted tool calls, in parallel. Typed tools reject URLs absent from the run's research sources. Hosted-search-only responses continue into reporting within the same step budget. The model extracts the evidence; source membership does not independently fact-check its summary. Dates are classified as current, recent, historical or unknown. Current needs a date range covering today. Recent needs a source showing the campaign running within the past 12 months, using its start date, end date or latest evidence date. The agent may use a publication date as the latest evidence date only when the source reports the campaign as launching or running then, and a date given only as a month or year counts as the first day of that period. Only matched subway stations or street addresses with current or recent dates affect competition. Geocoded areas and unknown or historical dates remain visible as markers without lowering gap scores. Other findings stay visible with source links, evidence and locations. A search returning no campaigns does not establish that competitors are absent. The sample recording contains five competitors and twenty campaign findings, nine of them with map locations. The Competitors tab ends with a "How the agent worked" section: the tools the agent called with counts (web search, open page, report competitor, report campaign, locate on map, and the two finish tools), then its reasoning summaries and each call in order, grouped by phase or competitor. Reasoning comes from OpenAI's `reasoningSummary: "auto"` and from the notes the model writes before searching; recorded research has no trace. Re-capture it from `tools/` with `uv run python -c 'from tools.sources.competitor_run import load; load(refresh=True)'` while the web app runs. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Count campaigns from the past 12 months as competition`: in the browser, the dating-app brief classified Hinge, The League and HER as running in the past 12 months, and The League's billboard at 41st Street and 7th Avenue, reported on 16 October 2026, made the Gap tab appear with the recent-advertising wording. The budgeting-app brief, with no recent campaign at a precise location, kept audience fit in that browser run, and a live run of the same brief through the API qualified a StreetEasy placement at Thompson Street and West Houston Street. The browser had no console errors from the app. All 49 tests, web lint, typecheck and build passed. Classic is selected by default and listed first. The teal and coral palette is ink text (#12211F, #5B6B69, #8A9694) on #FAFAF8 with #E3E8E7 dividers, a teal ramp (#BFE0DC #7FC2BA #2F8F86 #0B5450) and a coral accent (#F2603D, darker #C9431F); teal appears only in the map fill, the active layer tab and the legend bar. Teal and coral, blue and lime, purple and amber, and a colour-blind navy palette are the alternatives. Placement markers are 24px accent circles with a white ring, 30px and darker when selected, and merge into numbered groups when they overlap at the current zoom; the map frames the placements when they first arrive. Most customers lists the five neighbourhoods with the most tracts in the top 3%, with tract counts. Verified on 8 November 2026 in headless Chrome. Not an agreed product decision, only options to compare.
 - Built: competitor research with the Vercel AI SDK's `ToolLoopAgent`, OpenAI directly through `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and hosted web search and page reading. The research default is `gpt-5.6-luna`, selected in `AI_MODELS` in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`. Model names are not read from environment variables. Research runs in two stages. Discovery finds up to six competitors from the startup's product and target customer rather than its industry label: the model first writes short shopper phrases for the product and customer, then searches at least four times, recent campaign news first, for companies that have run New York subway, billboard, bus shelter, LinkNYC or wild-posting campaigns and that sell a substitute or target the same customer. Government campaigns, non-profits and media owners are excluded. Discovery also records every campaign its searches turn up, including ones that name no place, using recent campaigns and the current year in its searches. It cannot finish with fewer than three competitors until it has made five searches. Discovery has twelve model steps and a 60-second deadline. Each competitor then gets its own placement search for stations, street addresses, neighbourhoods and dates, told which campaigns are already recorded, with eight model steps and 65 seconds, all running concurrently within a 165-second total deadline; the Route Handler has a 170-second deadline. One finding can name up to six places, and each place becomes its own row. Each competitor can contribute up to six rows with a map location and three without, counted separately so that findings without a place cannot crowd out located ones. A run reports at most 54 rows. The first model step of each stage requires hosted search, and each response allows up to eight hosted tool calls, in parallel. Typed tools reject URLs absent from the run's research sources. Hosted-search-only responses continue into reporting within the same step budget. The model extracts the evidence; source membership does not independently fact-check its summary. Dates are classified as current, recent, historical or unknown. Current needs a date range covering today. Recent needs a source showing the campaign running within the past 12 months, using its start date, end date or latest evidence date. The agent may use a publication date as the latest evidence date only when the source reports the campaign as launching or running then, and a date given only as a month or year counts as the first day of that period. Only matched subway stations or street addresses with current or recent dates affect competition. Geocoded areas and unknown or historical dates remain visible as markers without lowering gap scores. Other findings stay visible with source links, evidence and locations. A search returning no campaigns does not establish that competitors are absent. The sample recording contains five competitors and twenty campaign findings, nine of them with map locations. The Competitors tab ends with a "How the agent worked" section: the tools the agent called with counts (web search, open page, report competitor, report campaign, locate on map, and the two finish tools), then its reasoning summaries and each call in order, grouped by phase or competitor. Reasoning comes from OpenAI's `reasoningSummary: "auto"` and from the notes the model writes before searching; recorded research has no trace. The budgeting-app brief, with no recent campaign at a precise location, kept audience fit in that browser run, and a live run of the same brief through the API qualified a StreetEasy placement at Thompson Street and West Houston Street. The budgeting app found Openigloo, StreetEasy and RentHop, and its Openigloo marathon campaign produced approximate markers at Fort Greene, Williamsburg, Greenpoint, Park Slope and the Upper East Side. The dating app found Plenty of Fish, Hinge, The League, Bumble, Cerca and HUD, with 12 campaign findings, four of them at matched subway stations. The budgeting app found Openigloo, StreetEasy and Job Today; the pizza delivery service found Slice, Seamless and WoodSpoon; the telehealth service found Roman. None of the findings had confirmed current dates, so none lowered gap scores. In the browser, the sample brief listed Openigloo, StreetEasy and RentHop with seven campaign findings and no console errors. All 32 tests, web lint, typecheck and build passed. Code defaults select OpenAI `gpt-5.6-luna` for research and Gateway Jev for audience decisions. Unsupported research providers are rejected until a compatible search adapter is added. Model environment variables have no effect; `.env.example` lists credentials only.  - LLM calls and AI agents: Vercel AI SDK in the web app. Jev uses Vercel AI Gateway. The competitor-campaign agent uses OpenAI directly through `@ai-sdk/openai` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`, as chosen by the user on 2026-11-07. The Python scripts in `tools/` call no language model. Python prepares the numerical dataset, and everything that depends on one startup's form runs in the web app. 2026-11-07.
 - AI model configuration: model defaults live in `AI_MODELS` in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`, so switching models requires one code edit and no model environment variables. The defaults are `openai:gpt-5.6-luna` for competitor research and `gateway:typesafe-ai/jev` for audience decisions. The user selected GPT-5.6 Luna for research on 2026-11-07. The Vercel AI SDK provider registry resolves both. The research adapter keeps its model, hosted search tools, provider options, credential checks, source decoding and error messages together. Audience scoring resolves a decision model separately. Environment variables supply credentials only. 2026-11-07.
 - Audience fit scoring: Jev, TypeSafe AI's decision model, scores the target-customer sentence against each column of the prebuilt tract dataset, and the web app weights the columns by those scores. Jev answers declared yes/no, choice and score questions with probabilities instead of writing text, and is called as `typesafe-ai/jev` through AI Gateway. The tract data is numbers, which code combines without a model, so Jev's part is turning the sentence into weights. Weights are signed, because the direction depends on the customer: a high income is good for an affluent audience and bad for a low-income one, and `median_age` points the opposite way for young and older audiences. The weighted score divides by the sum of the absolute weights, because signed weights can sum to zero and make a plain average unstable. One request costs about $0.00001. 2026-11-07.

It does not ask B2B or B2C, which the target customer covers. The form reads as one sentence, "Our company is … in …. We want to reach … who would pay $… per …", which fits shops, services and B2B companies as well as startups, and describes customers the company wants rather than ones it has (2026-11-08). Budget filters out placements with minimum spends, and what a customer pays stands in for lifetime value in the audience weighting because it is easier to answer. 2026-11-07.

 - Built: campaign location lookup with Geoapify, using `GEOAPIFY_API_KEY` on the server, and street corners from a table of New York intersections. Supported source-reported landmarks, neighbourhoods and street addresses are resolved within New York. A neighbourhood gets an approximate marker at the neighbourhood itself. Geoapify results that are only the borough, a business named after the area, or a street that shares the area's words are rejected, because it returned Brooklyn itself for "Fort Greene, Brooklyn", a veterinary clinic for "Upper East Side, Manhattan" and a Bronx street for "West Village". Street corners, written as "A and B", "A & B", "A at B", "corner of A and B" or "A between B and C", are looked up in `data/streets/intersections.csv`, 55,978 intersections built by `tools/src/tools/sources/streets.py` from NYC Open Data's street centerline, and get address precision. A corner found in several boroughs is placed only when the text names one of them or a neighbourhood in it, and a corner not in the table stays unmapped; neither is sent to Geoapify, whose free-text search returned Madison Avenue & East 41st Street for "41st Street & 7th Avenue".
